articles.title: Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers
articles.content: Welcome to LWN.net The following subscription-only content has been made available to you by an LWN subscriber. Thousands of subscribers depend on LWN for the best news from the Linux and free software communities. If you enjoy this article, please consider subscribing to LWN . Thank you for visiting LWN.net! By Joe Brockmeier November 10, 2026 Mike Lothian owns a docking station (or dock) that uses a DisplayLink chipset that had, at least in his opinion, subpar performance on Linux. He decided to try improving the Linux driver, with LLM assistance, but ran into one problem that he could not solve—so he asked for help, hoping that Synaptics's developers would lend a hand. (DisplayLink was acquired by Synaptics in 2022.) Rather than help him in improving the driver, however, the Synaptics legal team responded with patent infringement claims, a demand that he cease unauthorized implementation of DisplayLink technology, and threats of expensive legal penalties. For now, it appears that Linux users of the company's docks will have to continue to live without feature parity with other platforms. Synaptics and Displaylink The dock that he was trying to support is a Dell device that connects to a system via USB 3 and allows users to connect multiple monitors and other devices to their computer. It provides its DisplayLink Manager (DLM) software for Linux for the devices via an APT repository for Ubuntu. The company only provides DLM software in binary form, and only for x86-based platforms. The software is proprietary, but the company does maintain an open-source, out-of-tree kernel module that is included with DLM, the Extensible Virtual Display Interface (EVDI) project. It provides a driver that's compatible with Linux DRM and allows users to manage their docked displays with standard tools used for display settings, such as xrandr or GNOME and KDE Plasma's utilities. A short article explains why the company has not released source code for DLM: the software uses a proprietary graphics technology called DL3 to create a compressed stream of the various channels (e.g., USB, DisplayLink video, audio) over a communication channel (USB 3 in this case) and decode it again for output to the user's devices. Unfortunately, the vendor-supplied software did not work well for Lothian. I spoke and chatted with him via Signal while writing this article; he said that the driver kept crashing under Linux, so he decided to use his Claude subscription to try to develop a new driver and support software. Vino He posted the first patch series for Vino—his Rust-based DRM/KMS driver—to the kernel's dri-devel list as an RFC on June 17. Lothian noted that it was in an incomplete state, and asked for help with a blocker that he had run into trying to communicate with the dock's control plane. articles.title: After 7 months, Glasswing overwelms maintainers with underwhelming findings
articles.content: VulnCheck Community gives you free access to VulnCheck KEV, NVD++, Initial Access Community, and VulnCheck XDB Join Now Key Takeaways: Seven months into Project Glasswing, VulnCheck has tracked 442 CVEs attributable to Anthropic, roughly 0.5% of all CVEs published this year, with only two identified as exploited in the wild. Of Anthropic’s 37,966 reported findings, only 7,349 (19.4%) have been made public and just 217 have been marked fixed. Since September, Anthropic has added nearly 12,000 findings while recording just 15 additional fixes, widening the gap between discovery and remediation. Roughly 1,654 findings (4.4%) have been marked as duplicates, nearly eight times the number fixed, and another 419 have been withdrawn. Anthropic’s claimed true positive rate has risen from 90.8% to 94.2%, raising questions about how it accounts for duplicates and withdrawn findings. Anthropic’s OSS Scanner shifts validation work to maintainers, with curl rejecting 19 of 34 published reports as vulnerabilities, confirming six as low severity and leaving nine awaiting assessment. Also putting Anthropic's true positive rates into question. We're seven months into Anthropic's flagship Project Glasswing, and it's time for another update on the results. I've been tracking the project to see whether its claims are overhyped or grounded in reality. As we all recall, Anthropic launched Project Glasswing on April 7th, claiming, "We have identified thousands of additional high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities that we are working on responsibly disclosing to open source maintainers." What surprised me was how little evidence the project offered, which made me wonder whether this was more of an overhyped marketing campaign. That said, we shouldn't overlook that AI is an effective tool for finding vulnerabilities. But that story goes well beyond any single frontier model's capabilities. If you're just catching up, this builds on my earlier posts: So let's look at the results… I started tracking Anthropic's discovered vulnerabilities on April 17th, shortly after launch, in an open source repo called Anthropic Credited CVEs . The goal was to see whether Anthropic's claims lived up to the hype. This was before Anthropic launched its own disclosure ledger , which is only updated in infrequent bulk batches. My repo tracks every vulnerability attributable to Anthropic using CVE records, GHSAs, Linux kernel commits, and Anthropic's own ledger. I also manually audit advisories to catch CVEs that might otherwise get overlooked. After seven months, I've tracked 442 CVEs attributable to Anthropic. That's an average of just 63 per month. Out of the 93,450 CVEs published this year, that's only about 0.5% of all CVEs. For comparison, Anthropic's own public ledger lists just 217 fixed vulnerabilities, so I've tracked more than twice as many as Anthropic has disclosed itself. articles.title: Scion is back and is going to sell a kei truck in America
articles.content: When Toyota first introduced the Scion marque in 2003, it had one primary goal – sell cars to the younger generation. Its cars were cheaper and available in fun colors with fun names like “High Voltage Yellow” and “xPRESSO.” When I was a kid in the early 2000s, I often dreamed of one day owning a tC in Black Cherry Pearl and enjoyed lovingly calling xBs “toaster cars.” Over half of new Scions sold were to people under 35, and the tC boasted the youngest average buyer age in the entire industry at a sprightly 29. Their sales numbers peaked in 2006, but dropped nearly 75% by 2010. After sustained financial struggle, Toyota retired the marque in 2016. But now, a decade later, everyone’s favorite toaster brand is seemingly back. Today, Toyota announced the official revival of Scion, but instead of being a quirky and budget-conscious line, they are becoming Toyota’s cornerstone of curiosity. Now called “Scion by Toyota,” it is being launched as a “freedom lab” where drivers can, and are encouraged to challenge conventional ways of thinking about mobility through design, vehicle concepts, and features. “Okei,” let’s go. Toyota Their first production vehicle is the KEI-01, an ultra-compact utility truck, otherwise known as a kei truck. Toyota will be using its existing manufacturing infrastructure in Indiana to “produce” them for sale in the American market. “Produce” is in quotation marks because the KEI-01 is quite literally a rebadged Toyota Pixis, which is a rebadged Daihatsu Hijet Jumbo Cab. Based on its initial imagery it is seemingly also still right-hand drive, and there’s no word on if a LHD variant will be available in the future. With its friendly little 660cc engine and CVT transmission, the KEI-01 was certified to meet American low-speed vehicle safety standards, meaning it has a limited top speed of less than 25mph and is only legal on roads with a posted speed limit of less than 35mph. This makes it not really usable as a daily driver, but keeps it in this beautiful sweet spot where it has a shocking number of commercial and agricultural uses. Toyota The KEI-01 has a 600-pound payload (which means cargo and passengers) and a three-way fold-down cargo bed, making it a well-equipped workhorse for use on farms and in warehouses. It’s only about 5 feet wide and 11 feet long, which makes it great for use as a delivery or work vehicle in dense, urban areas like New York City. Believe it or not, it also has 4WD, which means it can traverse uneven terrain in more rural areas with ease. And don’t worry if it’s hot outside, because heat and air conditioning are standard. Toyota It’s worth noting that, while Kei trucks are currently sold new in the U.S. as “mini trucks” through independent distributors, this one is sold directly by Toyota. Before you rush to your local Toyota dealer to place a deposit, I’m going to have to burst your bubble a bit. articles.title: Smart home devices should work without the internet
articles.content: AI;DR: I wrote the first draft, AI helped me edit and rewrite it, and I made the final pass. The rules, setups, and talks are my own. TLDR; Nothing core in my house depends on a vendor’s server. If the internet goes down, the house keeps running. That’s been rule one for about ten years, and my other rules came out of it. This post has the rules, then both talks I’ve given on home automation, slide by slide. Why local My Nest integration worked until Google broke the API. That’s the failure I plan around now. The talks have a few more: a Samsung fridge showing a TLS certificate error on its own screen, and a Camp Chef grill controller that needs Wi-Fi to show you the temperature. Everything that matters runs on hardware I own. That’s Tasmota on ESP boards, an MQTT broker, and Node-RED on a Raspberry Pi. I do use some cloud services, mostly Alexa and a few AWS ones. Alexa is just another way to flip a switch. If it’s down, the wall switches and the wall dashboard still work. The rules From the first talk, restated in the second: No internet, no problem. Core stuff has to work with the internet unplugged. Alexa can be a way in, but never the only way. Don’t remove the old way while adding the new one. If someone tapes a wall switch on so a smart bulb keeps power, I skipped this rule. Be agile. Rooms get used differently and people move in and out, so it all has to be cheap to change. Check your automations. I once had four scheduled triggers hitting the same garden pump. Exceptions must be exceptional. I can break a rule, but only for a reason I’d still agree with six months later. Added after year five, once more people lived in the house: A cloud device needs an API with logs or it doesn’t get installed. I don’t want a black box in the house. Config lives in one place instead of five vendor apps. More than one way in: an app, Alexa, a QR code, or an NFC tag. If I keep doing the same steps, they become a routine. Devices talk pub/sub over MQTT instead of point to point. No batteries unless they last a year or more between changes. Nobody wants to swap a door sensor battery at 2am. The build I get asked about most is the Tasmota sprinkler controller . It’s in both talks, and so is the garage door setup, which has been running about as long. Talk One: Home Automation Nobody needs any of this. I like building things that just work in the background, and each automation is a small puzzle. Everything talks to a cloud now: phones, laptops, thermostats, locks. Those clouds may or may not be up when you need them, so know what you’re signing up for before you plug something in. Most people start here: a thermostat, a plug, a lock. Each has its own app and account. Every device lands somewhere on this triangle. A cloud camera is cheap and easy, and it costs you privacy. articles.title: AlphaProof Code
articles.content: How Google DeepMind researchers built a new agentic framework that formally verified the code of Signal’s cryptographic protocol — long considered to be a grand security challenge Today, we’re sharing a milestone in software security long considered to be a grand challenge: Google DeepMind researchers guided AI agents to mathematically prove key security properties of the actual code underlying the Signal protocol, the technology that protects billions of private conversations in apps like Signal and Google Messages. This breakthrough discovery was made using AlphaProof Code , a novel agentic framework for formal verification at unprecedented depth that combines human expertise with AI agents. Formal verification—mathematically proving code runs correctly without flaws—is the highest standard of security assurance; however, it is difficult and often labor-intensive. Our work marks the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth. It's also the first time the implementation of a widely deployed protocol like this has been formally verified by any method, with or without AI. How we verified Signal AlphaProof Code is a multi-LLM agentic framework that splits the work of formal verification the way a research team would: human experts work with AI to decide what to prove, and a group of AI agents does it. First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code. Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human – just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most. Cryptographic protocols underpin nearly all digital communication, from online banking to web browsing, and a single flaw can expose millions of people at once. That's why experts have spent decades formally analyzing them. But most protocol verification stops at the design level. Our agents went further, proving that the compiled code fulfills the key security properties – such as keeping messages protected before and after a device is temporarily compromised – down to the exact code running on devices. Because real-world vulnerabilities often hide in the gap between design and implementation, bridging this gap makes these proofs vastly more complex. Even at this complexity, our verification process took just four weeks – a task that historically takes expert teams years – proving that Signal's core cryptographic code delivers the security protections our experts specified. articles.title: Show HN: Get your coding agent off ~2019 JavaScript, onto modern web primitives
articles.content: Modern Web Guidance is a set of skills that embed web platform expertise, best practices, and browser compatibility data directly into your coding agents. It helps to steer your coding agents away from legacy patterns, and instead toward solutions that harness the power and capabilities of the modern web platform. Stewarded by the Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox, and MDN teams, alongside the web development community. Documentation · Eval Dashboard · Source Code · Report an Issue Quickstart npx modern-web-guidance@latest install This command runs an interactive wizard to install Modern Web Guidance. See Alternative Installation Methods below. Try it out (without installing) # Search for relevant guides npx modern-web-guidance@latest search " animate a dialog modal backdrop " # Retrieve a guide by ID npx modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve " animate-to-from-top-layer " # Scan a codebase for legacy patterns to modernize npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan . Why? Coding agents often default to older patterns because LLM training data contains vast amounts of legacy code. This often leads them to generate bloated JavaScript for tasks that now have native, high-performance web platform solutions. Even if a model knows an API exists, it often lacks the density of real-world, modern implementation patterns required for production-ready code. Modern Web Guidance bridges this gap. Our skill's CLI returns targeted, expert-curated guidelines directly into your agent's context window, focusing on: Modern Browser APIs : Helping models correctly structure APIs they frequently misuse. Performance & Accessibility : Preferring platform-level APIs that can be optimized by the browser and include built-in accessibility affordances. Responsible Fallbacks : Guiding models to use sensible, lightweight fallbacks instead of heavy polyfills or legacy libraries. What's Included? We cover the past several years of the web platform's new features, all the way up to the cutting edge. The guides are designed to be token-efficient ; we run evals enabling us to prune lowest-common-denominator content that models already know. Smooth visual states (View Transitions, entry/exit animations, parallax scroll, CSS scrollbar-color ). Modern layout systems (container queries, subgrid , modern color spaces like oklch , text-wrap tuning, and line-height trimming). Speed optimizations (instant preloading, Interaction to Next Paint (INP) diagnostics, and scheduling tasks via scheduler.yield ). Native components (Anchor Positioning for tooltips, Popover API, dialogs, :user-invalid validation, and auto-sizing fields). Important considerations (screen reader and keyboard operability, content navigation and discoverability). Local client models (native translation, summarization, and language detection APIs). articles.title: The hardest tarball
articles.content: The hardest tarball? Nov 7th, 2026 Here is a curiosity: an archive that can be constructed using a single GNU tar invocation, that is extracted in 8 distinct ways depending on what tool you use. $ printf hello > file $ touch empty $ tar --format=pax --pax-option='delete=?time,size:=512' \ --transform='s,^\./file$,café,' \ -cf hardest.tar file ./file empty It creates an archive hardest.tar from three files file ./file empty in sequence, where file is repeated so that GNU tar stores the second one as a hard link, and empty is empty. Exploiting the unique path of the second entry, the hard link is renamed to café . This triggers tar to create a pax header to store the file name as UTF-8. We add a size=512 record to the pax header, which overrides the default size=0 from the hard link. The value 512 is not a coincidence: it is exactly the size of a tar header. Visually, this archive has the following structure, with two basic interpretations based on whether a hard link can have a size or not. Now, POSIX says that data blocks for a hard link “may be included” in pax archives, but the implications of this are not entirely clear. So the 512 bytes after the hard link are its data, and not the header of empty as we archived it? How can a hard link have different contents from its previous counterpart file ? Extracting it This archive gives by far the richest and most surprising results I've encountered so far when extracting it with well-known tar utilities and libraries. The results below were produced using the latest releases of all packages at the time of writing. GNU tar, BusyBox, Python, Go and Perl This group is reasonable in principle: they ignore the size on the hard link, and extract file , its hard link café , and empty . bsdtar This is the system tar utility of macOS, which is closer to POSIX in spirit regarding the concept of size on hard links, and writes the 512 bytes into the hard link. The end result is that file now contains the tar header of empty . 7-Zip, node-tar, tar-fs, and Rust's tar & astral-tokio-tar This group agrees with bsdtar that the 512 bytes are data of the hard link, but doesn't write them into the hard link. Instead, they skip forward over the data, and you are left with just file and café , without empty . Java's Commons Compress This is where you begin to need more imagination. Because café contains data, a separate file is created that contains the header of empty as data, while file keeps its original contents. PHP's PharData Makes café a separate, empty file, and also extracts empty . Why not? RubyGems Does not extract café at all, but to make up for it, it creates an empty directory PaxHeaders next to file and empty . R R has an entirely different approach: it extracts empty with 512 null bytes. It mistakenly applies the size to empty instead of the hard link, and those 512 bytes are from an end-of-archive marker. articles.title: Open Graph images with Astro and Typst
articles.content: Links to blog articles look better when they’re accompanied by an image. If the HTML head has a meta tag like this, it will happen automatically: < meta property = "og:image" content = "https://eaj.no/posts/graph-images-with-typst/og.png" /> My previous, tedious workflow for these kinds of images was to go to unspash.com , search for something like structure or archive , and then select an image I thought would fit the theme of the post. Being both boring and error-prone, I abandonded that process and set up a pipeline that generates image cards at build-time instead. They look like this: Let me show you how I did it. Typst Typst is a tool that generates high-quality documents from a simple markup language. A lovechild of LaTeX and Markdown , it works great for math whilst also keeping the day-to-day text formatting syntax bearable. As a small taste, this snippet (adapted from the Typst README ) #set page ( width : 10cm , height : auto , margin : 1cm ) #set heading ( numbering : "I." ) #let fib_1 = 1 #let fib_2 = 1 = The Fibonacci sequence The Fibonacci sequence is defined through the recurrence relation $ F _ n = F _ ( n-1 ) + F _ ( n-2 ) $ , with $ F _ 1 = #fib_1 $ and $ F _ 2 = #fib_2 $ . It can also be expressed in _closed form:_ $ F _ n = round ( 1 / sqrt ( 5 ) phi . alt ^ n ) , quad phi . alt = (1 + sqrt ( 5 ) ) / 2. $ produces this fine document: By default the typst CLI will create a PDF, but it can also make PNGs. The above image was created with the command typst compile \ --format png \ --ppi 250 \ typst-example.typ But if you’d rather create something with a bit more pizzazz, by all means. How about #set page ( width : 1200pt , height : 630pt , margin : 80pt , fill : rgb ( "#FF1493" )) #set text ( font : "Comic Sans MS" , fill : white , lang : "no" ) #grid ( rows : ( 1fr , auto ) , align ( left + horizon , { text ( size : 72pt , weight : 800 , "Typst very nice" ) }) , text ( size : 24pt , "Would typst again" ) , ) which yields Fantastic. If all of my posts were titled “Typst very nice”, we’d be done, but, alas. Luckily, typst accepts inputs to a document with --input key=value , which is put in a sys.inputs dictionary for the template to read. So the template becomes #set page ( width : 1200pt , height : 630pt , margin : 80pt , fill : rgb ( "#FF1493" )) #set text ( font : "Comic Sans MS" , fill : white , lang : "no" ) #let title = sys . inputs . at ( "title" , default : "You forgot the title :(" ) // Reading the input here ☝️ #grid ( rows : ( 1fr , auto ) , align ( left + horizon , { text ( size : if title . len () > 70 { 60pt } else { 72pt } , weight : 800 , title , ) }) , text ( size : 24pt , "Would typst again" ) , ) which, when rendered with typst compile \ --format png \ --ppi 144 \ --input title="Look ma, from the CLI!" fancy-typst-with-input.typ becomes Perfection. articles.title: You should try Gleam
articles.content: Introduction If you have read my recent rant about programming languages , you'll know I've been quite interested in Gleam . Gleam is a functional language that targets BEAM, the Erlang VM, with a simple syntax and interoperability with the wider BEAM ecosystem (Erlang and Elixir). Interestingly, Gleam can also target JavaScript i.e., Gleam can be compiled into JavaScript and run through Node.js. I've been mostly using Rust for hobby projects, which at the moment is the only language that really makes coding enjoyable for me, and Gleam has managed to scratch that itch too. If you're a Rust connaisseur , then Gleam will feel familiar to you, bar a few key differences. I feel like 80% of the code I write could be copy pasted to Rust (with a tinge of search-and-replace for syntax) and it'd compile. This post won't give an exhaustive overview of the language, if you want to learn more, I recommend the excellent interactive tour . You'll get a good feel for Gleam in under half an hour. Gleam: the good On its homepage, Gleam is described as "a friendly language for building type-safe systems that scale !" (emphasis theirs) which does a good job of conveying what Gleam is all about. Gleam is friendly The syntax is extremely simple, most of the complex stuff is hidden by the Erlang runtime which you don't really have to interact with unless you want to! Of course, Gleam is a functional language, so if you have lived in a C-shaped imperative world your whole life, it might be a bit daunting at first. But if you compare it to other functional languages (OCaml, Haskell, Erlang), you'll quickly notice Gleam is much simpler. After using it a bit, it feels like all the functional parts of Rust, with a few missing ones, and none of the imperative parts. articles.title: Microsoft are rejecting your mail
articles.content: On Friday morning, we became aware that a significant amount of email to Microsoft-run mail systems was being rejected. This included mail to hotmail.com and outlook.com. The messages were being rejected with the following message: 550 5.7.1 Message rejected: Message lacks SPF/DKIM/DMARC Auth Records We checked our logs, and found that we’d seen this message over 500 times on Thursday, but not once before that. The affected messages all had completely valid SPF and DKIM , but did not have a DMARC record. We added a DMARC record with a “none” policy to some of the affected domains, and sure enough, mail was then accepted again. A quick fedi-survey confirmed that we were not alone. DMARC records are a way of publicly stating what you want recipients to do with email that claims to be from your domain, but which doesn’t pass verification checks (DKIM or SPF) and thus is potentially forged. Your DMARC policy can be one of the following: reject – recipients should reject mail that doesn’t pass DKIM or SPF. This is the real purpose of DMARC: if you’re confident that all legitimate outbound mail is properly authenticated, you can tell recipients to assume that anything else is forged, and bin it. quarantine – recipients should treat such mail as suspicious. none – your domain has no policy on what to do with mail that doesn’t pass DKIM or SPF. Publishing a policy of none is effectively the same as not publishing a policy at all. Microsoft are now rejecting mail without a DMARC policy, but accepting mail with a policy of none . This is a massive and pointless change in their policy for incoming mail, made with no notice whatsoever. Last year Microsoft, introduced a policy that required domains sending more than 5,000 messages per day to have a DMARC record. This change was announced in advance . This latest change appears to be completely unannounced, which makes us wonder if it was even intentional. Of course, trying to contact Microsoft in order to resolve mail issues such as this is futile. Update: apparently it wasn’t intentional, but they haven’t figured out how to roll it back yet. We’ve just applied p=none DMARC records to a large number of our customers’ domains. We generally try to avoid making unsolicited changes to DNS zones, but in this case we feel that it is the best option. If you’re in contact with Microsoft users affected by this, please encourage them to complain to Microsoft; it’s very likely that they are losing other legitimate email from other providers because of this unannounced change. Better still, encourage them to move to an email provider that is pro-active in investigating email deliverability issues .

articles.title: I deleted all my SSH keys
articles.content: I’ve been using ed25519-sk keys with YubiKeys since practically the moment they were available. But because of some specific use-cases (and because, frankly, YubiKeys are expensive) I’ve had a few traditional on-disk keys hanging around for a while just waiting for me to finally decide to get rid of them. This post documents how I’m using various secure enclaves (YubiKey, TPM, Apple Secure Enclave) to hold/encrypt SSH key material and achieve the goal of not having any unprotected key material living on-disk. First – Isn’t using a passphrase enough? Probably. I don’t intend to imply that this post is the only way that anyone should be doing SSH keys. Using a passphrase will encrypt the key with bcrypt & AES which keeps it protected even if the on-disk keyfile leaks somehow. And with a functioning ssh-agent, the passphrase should only need to be entered once per session, with the decrypted key material being held in RAM after that point. So yes, the ’traditional’ method is probably fine for most threat models. But I’m still keen to move to hardware-backed keys anyway, mostly for the satisfaction. About hardware-resident keys When I say ‘hardware-resident’ keys, I mean keys that use a secure enclave or purpose-built hardware like YubiKeys to store or protect the key material. The theoretical benefit here is that the hardware used to generate the SSH key is needed in order to use the key. There’s no mechanism that allows leaking or exfiltrating keys that generated using this method. Any material that does exist on-disk is useless without the hardware. Goals So I want to: Switch to using hardware-resident keys entirely Do so as natively as possible, avoiding additional software where I can Test these in various real-world scenarios, such as running within an LXC or noninteractively mounting an SSHFS server Hardware I’m going to try three different hardware methods for achieving this, which I think will cover all of my needs: Method 1: YubiKey Method 2: TPM Method 3: Apple Secure Enclave Method 1: YubiKey With a YubiKey (5 and newer), SSH keys can be directly enrolled into the device using ed25519-sk (where the -sk stands for “Security Key”). This doesn’t require any additional software beyond OpenSSH itself. To store a new SSH key on a YubiKey, insert it and run: ssh-keygen -t ed25519-sk -O resident -O application = "ssh:yournamehere" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519-sk The application tag set in the command is arbitrary and can be set to whatever memorable string you prefer to differentiate between multiple SSH keys if you want to create multiple keys on the same YubiKey. If you have ykman installed, you can now inspect the list of credentials enrolled in the device: $ ykman fido credentials list Enter your PIN: Credential ID RP ID Username Display name 0f41fb61... ssh:yournamehere openssh openssh If ykman complains that you haven’t set a FIDO PIN on the YubiKey yet, you can do this with ykman fido access change-pin . articles.title: Weird licenses and the new open source
articles.content: Somewhere on an IRC channel, I ended up in a conversation about the The Filthy Human Hands (FHH) License . It wasn't the first time weird licenses were discussed there: Reticulum 's sparked some interesting discussions as well. Let's start from the beginning. If you don't want to read the Wikipedia article on Free Software , a couple of years ago, I gave a small presentation at school as part of the "Oral communication in English" course, which is a (shoddy) cake-based explanation of the topic. Long story short, a Free Software is a software with 4 freedoms: The freedom to run the program as you wish, for any purpose. The freedom to study how the program works, and change it to make it do what you wish. Access to the source code is a precondition for this. The freedom to redistribute copies so you can help others. The freedom to distribute copies of your modified versions to others. By doing this you can give the whole community a chance to benefit from your changes. There is also the term Open Source, which is more or less Free Software but without the sociopolitical aspect of it, which is like a pizza without olives, or art without context: something devoid of meaning, a business-oriented product instead of a creation. Like in every sociopolitical endeavour, people sometimes disagree, leading to subtle but important variations. One of the most important one in the Free Software movement has been the question of the copyleft : should derivatives of Free Software be licensed under the same license? Some licenses, like the GPL says yes and this includes everything built on top of GPL code, the LGPL says that only code under LGPL needs to be released as LGPL, and others, called permissive licenses, like the BSD and MIT don't impose such restrictions. The Free Software movement started in 1986, so we're around 40 years later now, and the picture is pretty bleak: technically, one could argue that it won, as every computer-using company in the world depends on Free Software one way or the other: Firefox, Linux, VLC, Chrome, Ubuntu, Apache, nginx, Wikipedia, Open Street Map, Open Food Facts, … as well as more fundamental software components like curl, libxml, busybox, OpenSSL, GCC, clang, … Yet virtually none of them do contribute back to those commons, some of them being thanklessly maintained by a random person in Nebraska . Worse, a handful of computer-related companies ("cloud providers") are making ungodly amount of money renting infrastructure running Free Software, most smart™ devices are running Free Software, every single software producing/selling company depends on Free Software, and again, almost none contribute back meaningfully. A small number are trying to sponsor some projects they're depending on, but it often feels like a crass move for software that are maintained as a hobby: "Could you please garden a bit more efficiently, and add 150 apple trees to your small garden? We need it for our business, here is a 1000€ one-time payment" Wi

The rules for Easter were broadly decided at the First Council of Nicaea, organised by Emperor Constantine in 325 AD, ultimately landing on the first Sunday after the first full moon, on or after March 21 . Later, for operational efficiency, the church defined "full moon" according to a formula, which was eventually modified by Pope Gregory XIII in 1582 ("Gregorian Easter") , with the first Easter under the new rules applying in most Catholic countries the following year. The Church of England first observed the new date of Easter in 1753, but Eastern / Orthodox churches continue to follow the old rules. This article is about the new "Gregorian" Easter, because it is much more complex and slow to compute. articles.title: vercel-labs/agent-browser (Rust)
articles.content: Browser automation for AI agents: open pages, read them as an accessibility tree, and act on elements from the shell. agent-browser is a native Rust CLI that gives an AI agent a browser it can drive one command at a time. snapshot returns the page as compact text with a ref such as @e1 for each element. The agent acts on a ref, reads the page again to check the result, and repeats. The browser stays open between commands, so each step is one short shell call. npm install -g agent-browser agent-browser install # download Chrome for Testing (first time only) Homebrew: brew install agent-browser , then agent-browser install . Linux: agent-browser install --with-deps also installs the browser's system libraries. No install: npx agent-browser open example.com . Project installs, building from source, upgrade , and doctor are covered in Installation . agent-browser open example.com agent-browser snapshot -i # interactive elements, each with a ref agent-browser click @e1 # act on a ref from that snapshot agent-browser get url # check the result agent-browser close The snapshot for example.com : - link "Learn more" [ref=e1] Refs describe the page at the time of the snapshot. After navigation or a DOM change, take a new snapshot before using refs again. CSS selectors, text, XPath, and semantic locators also work, for example agent-browser find role button click --name "Submit" . See Selectors . A click fails, instead of reporting success, when the target is hidden, disabled, outside the viewport, or covered by another element such as a consent banner. Dismiss the covering element, take a new snapshot, and retry. The full walkthrough is in the quick start . The CLI sends each command to a background daemon that starts on the first command and controls the browser over the Chrome DevTools Protocol. Each --session gets its own daemon and browser. By default, the daemon closes a headless browser and exits after one hour without commands, saving state first when session persistence is configured. Chrome for Testing is the default browser. You can also attach to a running Chrome with --cdp or --auto-connect ( CDP mode ), select the Lightpanda or Obscura engine with --engine , drive Mobile Safari in the iOS Simulator , or use a cloud browser provider such as Browserbase , Browserless , Browser Use , Kernel , or AgentCore . articles.summary: 基准测试显示，投票与自我纠错等 LLM 可靠性层只能筛除可疑输出，无法恢复准确率，确定性查表更可靠。

articles.title: Google Cloud Spend Caps Reach General Availability with API and Monthly Resets
articles.content: Google Cloud has made spend caps on Cloud Billing Budgets generally available, pausing new usage of a service in a project once a monthly budget is hit, without deleting resources. GA adds an API, estimated live costs, and automatic monthly resets, but caps cover only the Gemini API, the Agent Platform, Cloud Run, and Cloud Run functions, and overages during enforcement delays are still billed. By Steef-Jan Wiggers
articles.summary: Google Cloud 预算支出上限正式可用，达月度预算即暂停服务用量，新增 API 与自动重置，但仅覆盖部分服务。

articles.title: Effect 4.0 Ships: Dependency-Free Rewrite with 5x Smaller Bundles and Long-Term Support
articles.content: Effect 4.0, a TypeScript framework for typed errors and structured concurrency, was released on 30 September 2026 with a rewritten fiber runtime. The team reports a bundle size drop from 35.6 kB to 7.1 kB and about 6.4x higher throughput, though these figures are not independently verified. It also adds long-term support through September 2029. By Daniel Curtis
articles.summary: TypeScript 框架 Effect 4.0 发布，重写运行时实现零依赖，包体积从 35.6kB 降至 7.1kB，并提供长期支持。

articles.title: Java News Roundup: TornadoVM, A2A Java, Open Liberty, Open J Proxy, Gradle, EclipseStore
articles.content: This week's Java roundup for November 2nd, 2026, features news highlighting: point releases of TornadoVM, TornadoInsight, A2A for Java, Gradle and EclipseStore; the November 2026 edition of Open Liberty; the third release candidate of Open J Proxy; the second release candidates of Micrometer Metrics and Micrometer Tracing; and the third beta release of Quarkus 4.0. By Michael Redlich
articles.summary: 本周 Java 生态动态：TornadoVM、A2A Java、Gradle 等发布新版本，Open Liberty 与 Open J Proxy 推出候选版本。

articles.title: Google Releases Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics Control, Simulation, and Policy Improvement
articles.content: Google has released Gemini 4 Argon framing it as a general-purpose physical-reasoning model for robot control, Real2Sim scene construction, multimodal labeling of robot video, and iterative policy improvement, rather than as a single end-effector policy. By Daniel Dominguez
articles.summary: Google 发布 Gemini 4 Argon，定位通用物理推理模型，用于机器人控制、Real2Sim 场景构建与策略迭代优化。

articles.title: Cloudflare Develops Public Certificate Authority for Post-Quantum Web Security
articles.content: Cloudflare is developing a public certificate authority for Merkle Tree Certificates (MTCs) to reduce the bandwidth overhead of post-quantum cryptography. A Chrome experiment served billions of MTCs to 50% of Chrome Beta 146 for selected domains, reporting 9% faster median performance. Wider deployment depends on browser support, transparency, and production-scale validation. By Leela Kumili
articles.summary: Cloudflare 开发面向后量子安全的公共证书颁发机构，用 Merkle Tree 证书降低带宽开销，Chrome 实验显示中位性能提升 9%。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #542: AI week ahead: data center pause backers could win 15 governor races
articles.content: This issue is about the week ahead, and something is scheduled almost every day. On Tuesday, US voters choose 36 governors, and in up to 15 of those races the candidate who backs a pause on new data centers could win. Apple reports earnings today and AMD on Tuesday. On Wednesday, Apple starts testing Apple Intelligence in China with Alibaba's Qwen, and Agility Robotics expects to close its deal to go public. When Congress returns on November 9, OpenAI plans to push for "speed limits" on the most powerful AI. Last week, a fake Claude Code update reached up to 5,000 Cursor users, and in a Cornell and Yale test nine of ten AI models raised their own spending limits. In the middle: insuring Big Tech's debt now costs more than at any time since 2021.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 展望本周：美国 36 州州长选举中，最多 15 场支持暂停新建数据中心的候选人可能胜出，苹果、AMD 将发布财报。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #541: Big Tech reports AI spending Wednesday as CoreWeave debt hits distress
articles.content: This issue looks ahead. On Wednesday the Fed announces its rate decision, then Microsoft and Alphabet report after the close. Amazon follows on Thursday. Investors want to know whether AI spending is still paying off, and the credit market is already nervous: insurance against a CoreWeave default now costs more than 10% a year. Anthropic is expected to file its IPO paperwork publicly any day. Moonshot says Kimi K3.1 Pro's open weights arrive November 4. Israel votes on Tuesday after a campaign full of AI deepfakes, and the US midterms are a week from Tuesday. In the middle: so far, AI has paid off for the companies that sell it, not the ones that buy it.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 预告微软、Alphabet、亚马逊将发布财报，投资者关注 AI 支出回报，CoreWeave 债务违约保险成本已升至困境水平。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #540: AI is finding software flaws faster than teams can fix them
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past two weeks, drawn from our Use-Case Library and from SEC filings. Three things stand out: AI now finds security flaws at record volume, AI agents do a large share of the work at some companies, and test agents keep doing things nobody asked them to do.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 应用版指出，AI 发现安全漏洞的速度已超过团队修复能力，部分公司大量工作由 AI 代理完成，测试代理持续增多。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #539: AI-made midterm ads top $137 million, and 70% carry no AI label
articles.content: Campaigns and PACs have spent more than $137 million on AI-generated or AI-enhanced midterm ads, and about 70% of them carry no AI label, the New York Times reported. The biggest pro-AI super PAC network paid about $20 million to a Nevada company that exists only as a post office box. A new report found 81 of 134 AI models failed a test built from terrorist-style questions. A video game reverse engineering site is closing because AI made the work too easy. Some companies that rushed into AI are now limiting it, and a JAMA study counted 270 million questions doctors asked one AI tool. In the middle: police in Michigan used an AI-generated photo of a teenager to catch a suspect.
articles.summary: 据纽约时报报道，AI 生成或增强的中期选举广告支出超 1.37 亿美元，约 70% 未标注 AI，最大亲 AI 超级 PAC 向空壳公司支付约 2000 万美元。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #537: AI models may soon copy themselves onto smart fridges, Anthropic says
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared most since our last issue on October 8, minus the stories we already sent you in the Daily Espresso. The most shared: Anthropic's warning that small AI models may soon be able to copy themselves onto home devices. Also: a large study of what AI coding agents change at real companies, a fight over how to check AI math proofs, creative workers pushing back on AI, and police buying more AI.
articles.summary: Anthropic 警告小型 AI 模型可能很快能自我复制到智能冰箱等家用设备，这是 AI 专家近期分享最多的消息之一。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #536: Top AI models failed a test of inventing new AI research
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared over the past three days. Most of them look ahead: whether AI can do AI research on its own, who gets a say in governing it, how it is moving into war planning, and how it is moving onto personal computers.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 汇总专家关注点：顶尖 AI 模型未能通过自主开展新 AI 研究的测试，同时 AI 正进入治理、战争规划和个人电脑领域。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #535: AI got too expensive, so companies are moving to cheaper models
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past three weeks. Three patterns stand out: companies switching models to control cost, large deployments that are now in daily use, and a growing list of places where AI was restricted or removed.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 应用版观察到，AI 成本过高促使企业转向更便宜的模型，大型部署已进入日常使用，同时 AI 受限或被移除的场景增多。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #534: Universities cannot grade their way out of AI
articles.content: This week, campus IT leaders voted AI their top priority for the first time, Cambridge refused Turnitin's new terms over AI training on student work, Dartmouth opened an investigation into its own provost's writing, and Ken Griffin gave Carnegie Mellon $3 billion. Student AI use is no longer a future scenario. The useful question for universities is whether they can teach students to work with AI and still certify what those students can do without it. New evidence from tutoring trials, assessment redesigns, student-support systems and campus data deals points to a practical answer.
articles.summary: 高校 IT 负责人首次将 AI 列为首要任务，剑桥因 Turnitin 用学生作业训练 AI 拒绝新条款，达特茅斯调查教务长写作，AI 使用已非未来议题。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #533: Meta tested human callers behind its AI phone agent
articles.content: The AI story of September 22–28 was not simply that agents became more capable. It was that their hidden handoffs became visible: a supposedly automated call could reach a contractor, a supposedly private prompt or image could reach a reviewer, a monitor could detect an agent long before a person stopped it, and a local app flaw could inherit every permission a user had granted. The new AI Weekly Who’s Who census points to one practical question: when an agent crosses a boundary, who knows—and who can still intervene?
articles.summary: Meta 被曝其 AI 电话代理背后有真人接线员，AI 代理的隐藏人工转接、提示词与图像外泄等问题在 9 月下旬集中暴露。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #531: AI labs shipped agents before agreeing how to report failures
articles.content: The AI story of September 14–20 was not one spectacular model launch. It was the machinery around agents becoming visible: people reading private chats, models writing instructions into their own memory, plugins updating beneath users, and regulators asking how to stop a system after release. The latest AI Weekly Who’s Who census surfaced 535 expert-shared links. We ranked them by consequence and reader relevance, not by raw share count. Here is what mattered last week—and, more importantly, what could move the story from September 22–28.
articles.summary: AI 实验室在未就故障上报方式达成一致前就发布代理，私人聊天被阅读、模型自写记忆指令、插件静默更新等问题引发监管关注。

articles.title: We now have Kerr’s Law
articles.content: Dave Kerr created hacker laws, and now he finds himself reviewing agent-written code for them. Back on the show after six years, Dave names what he sees limiting teams today: keeping everyone’s mental model in sync with what’s actually been built. Adam declares it Kerr’s Law on the spot. We get into why Dave’s team treats code review as a deliberate slowdown, how Shellwright lets agents bring evidence to a pull request, and what living with bipolar disorder has taught Dave about noticing when the excitement of these tools stops being healthy.
articles.summary: Dave Kerr 重返节目，提出“Kerr 定律”：当前限制团队的是让所有人的心智模型与实际构建成果保持同步，尤其在代理写代码时代。

articles.title: The future is Postgres
articles.content: Craig Kerstiens returns to talk about the ever-expanding world of Postgres: a deliberately boring core, a thriving extension ecosystem, and pg_lake bringing DuckDB and Iceberg into the mix. We dig into the pain of ETL, what Craig is watching in Postgres 19, the impact of AI on open source maintainers, and why the database still has plenty of room to grow.
articles.summary: Craig Kerstiens 谈 Postgres 生态：核心刻意保持简单，扩展生态繁荣，pg_lake 引入 DuckDB 和 Iceberg，并讨论 AI 对开源维护者的影响。

articles.title: Building what's next
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Zeno Rocha, CEO of Resend, about scaling "boring" email to 3 million users, the secret Go rewrite behind it, and building for agents. We cover pricing.md, MCP, spam gangs, and why Resend keeps what's next for email.
articles.summary: Resend CEO Zeno Rocha 谈将“无聊”的邮件服务扩展至 300 万用户、背后的 Go 重写、面向代理构建，以及定价、MCP 和垃圾邮件团伙。

articles.title: From zero to NanoClaw
articles.content: Gavriel Cohen, creator of NanoClaw and co-founder of NanoCo, joins Adam to explain how a 40-hour weekend project became a viral open source hit and the foundation of an enterprise AI company. Gavriel describes the security concerns that led him to build a small, container-isolated alternative to OpenClaw, why he released it under the MIT license, and why the project's community and credibility are more valuable than keeping its code private. They explore the shift from writing code to architecting the environments in which agents work, NanoClaw's "skills over features" approach, the approval and governance layers required inside large companies, and a future where every worker manages agents without surrendering human judgment. They close with the technical simplicity behind NanoClaw, containers, TypeScript, SQLite, and a two-database design, and Adam's case for durable Agent Flow artifacts that keep organizational context from disappearing into chat.
articles.summary: Gavriel Cohen 讲述 40 小时周末项目 NanoClaw 如何成为病毒式开源爆款，并因安全顾虑打造容器隔离的小型 OpenClaw 替代品，进而创立企业 AI 公司。

articles.title: Forking Cal.com to closed source
articles.content: This week I'm joined by Peer Richelsen, co-founder of Cal.com. What if the majority of open source repositories are already compromised and we just don't know it yet? That's the theory Peer brings to the table this week. We dig into how AI has flattened the knowledge graph to the point that a 16-year-old can vibe hack a power station just as easily as their mom can vibe code an iOS app, why the reporting culture that has kept open source safe all these years is collapsing under AI generated noise, Cal.com's move to fork its own codebase and take the sensitive parts private, and the eye opening reality that shipping "$1 of AI tokens for pennies on the dollar" is now a common startup business model.
articles.summary: Cal.com 联合创始人 Peer Richelsen 提出多数开源仓库可能已被攻陷的猜想，并讨论 AI 如何压平知识图谱、以及 Cal.com 转向闭源。

articles.title: Postgres at PlanetScale
articles.content: Sam Lambert is back after 4 years and he does not hold back! We cover $5 PlanetScale Postgres, the Neki "do-over" of Vitess, agents shipping schema changes through deploy requests, rolling back a 500TB table in seconds, and the very real question of whether to open source any of it. Plus: why he thinks the sleeping, lazy giants should be broken up.
articles.summary: PlanetScale CEO Sam Lambert 谈 5 美元 Postgres、Vitess 重做、代理通过部署请求提交 schema 变更、秒级回滚 500TB 表及是否开源。

articles.title: Canary tokens and digital tripwires
articles.content: Haroon Meer is back! Haroon is the Founder of Thinkst, the ~50-person bootstrapped company behind Canary and Canarytokens — honeypots and tripwires you sprinkle inside your network and forget about until an attacker touches one. We talk about the AWS API key token attackers just can't resist trying, the real credit card token backed by an actual bank partnership, Breadcrumbs (their brand-new feature that leads intruders straight to your canaries), a live demo where a hardware Canary becomes a Synology NAS in one click, and how a company with zero outbound sales and no price increase in ten years quietly passed $22.5 million in ARR.
articles.summary: Thinkst 创始人 Haroon Meer 谈 Canary 与 Canarytokens 蜜罐和数字绊线，包括攻击者忍不住尝试的 AWS API 密钥诱饵。

articles.title: From open source hits to OpenAI
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Max Stoiber, currently working on ChatGPT's plugin directory and app platform at OpenAI. We discuss the hundreds of open source projects nobody remembers alongside the big ones like react-boilerplate and styled-components, how Spectrum became part of GitHub and eventually helped shape GitHub Discussions, the founder growth that came from building Stellate, the GraphQL cache that turned into a dual acquisition by Shopify and The Guild, and why ChatGPT apps feel like a new surface for software.
articles.summary: Max Stoiber 谈从 react-boilerplate、styled-components 等开源项目到 Spectrum 并入 GitHub，如今在 OpenAI 负责 ChatGPT 插件目录与应用平台。

articles.title: MCP on Code Mode
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Matt Carey about Code Mode and how most of us have been thinking about MCP all wrong. Matt works on the Agents SDK and MCP at Cloudflare — we discuss how server-side Code Mode lets one MCP server expose all ~2,500 Cloudflare API endpoints in about 1,000 tokens of context, the dynamic Worker loader that runs model-written code safely in a V8 isolate, Matt's own workflow with Claude, where memory fits into the future of agents, and his Zaggy git wrapper that keeps agents from force-pushing his repos.
articles.summary: Cloudflare 的 Matt Carey 介绍服务端 Code Mode，让单个 MCP 服务器以约 1000 token 上下文暴露全部约 2500 个 API 端点。

articles.title: Google Fi Brings Back Network Switching With 'Secondary' Partner
articles.content: Google Fi is bringing back network switching through an unnamed "secondary" 5G carrier. "Most users will be on the 'Primary network,' but Google Fi will automatically switch users to the 'Secondary network' if it meaningfully improves performance with so-called 'smart thresholds' for doing so," reports 9to5Google. "At launch, there is no manual switching." When Project Fi first launched the service included support with both Sprint and T-Mobile. That went away when T-Mobile acquired Sprint in 2020. 9to5Google reports: Google is not naming the second network today, but did share that Ultra Wideband is supported. Officially, you are switching between "two of America's fastest 5G networks." Fi Wireless does note that users have top priority, so data is never deprioritized on the Primary network. Meanwhile, there's "highest QCI priority" on the backup network that means subscribers are among the last to be slowed down when there's congestion. This is also available internationally when local partner networks are available with the Flexible and Unlimited Premium plans. Network switching will first be supported on Pixel 9 and newer devices that have a Google Fi eSIM (and no other SIM active). It makes use of Android's Multiple Enabled Profiles (MEP) eSIM technology that allows for two carrier profiles on a single chip. [...] These Google Fi updates start rolling out today, with network switching seeing gradual availability. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: Google Fi 重新引入网络切换，新增未具名二级 5G 运营商，性能明显提升时自动切换。

articles.title: Fireworks AI Confirms Wider Breach Affecting Notion AI Chats
articles.content: Fireworks AI says its October breach was broader than initially disclosed, with attackers gaining access to customer account and billing information as well as some datasets, incomplete model weights and secrets. Notion, the popular productivity and note-taking app, disclosed that it was impacted in the breach but "fewer than 1% of Notion workspaces" were involved. "Upon analysis of the new data, we discovered that it included Notion AI chat transcripts used for the Insights feature, which for the vast majority of impacted workspaces were unattributable," it said. "'Unattributable' means the chats weren't labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from, and the transcripts did not contain tool call results." The Hacker News reports: In a notice published on October 10, 2026, [Fireworks AI] said it detected unauthorized use of internal Fireworks credentials that allowed an unauthorized third-party to access environment variables used in evaluation jobs in a limited number of customer accounts. The activity was detected on October 6, 2026, at 9 a.m. PDT. [...] The latest bulletin from the company reveals that the scope of the breach may have been broader than previously thought. The company said attackers reached its development environment via an unnamed third-party cloud provider that hosted Fireworks research and development (R&D) machines on October 23, 2026. "On October 24, the unauthorized third party used it to reach Fireworks development machines and then run an unauthorized workload that led to additional customer data impact," it added. "As of October 25, we have not detected further evidence of successful unauthorized access by the threat actor on the Fireworks platform customers use." The breach is said to have provided access to the following types of information: [Resource metadata; Billing information; and Model weights and datasets]. Fireworks AI said payment card numbers are not stored by the company and were not impacted by the security
articles.summary: Fireworks AI 确认十月泄露范围扩大，攻击者获取客户账户、账单信息及部分数据集和模型权重，Notion AI 聊天受影响。

articles.title: New York Launches Nation's First State AI Testing Program
articles.content: New York is launching a state-backed AI safety research center at Binghamton University that will independently study and test AI systems, develop safety and security techniques, and train researchers in responsible AI. "While the federal government fails to act, New York is leading the way on AI safety and holding big tech accountable," New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said. "The stakes are too high to simply take AI companies at their word." Politico reports: The center -- which is funded by a $30 million gift from Bloomberg co-founder Tom Secunda and a $25 million research investment from SUNY and New York state -- is set to launch before New York's major AI safety law, the RAISE Act, comes into effect on Jan. 1. That will require submissions of detailed safety frameworks from AI companies operating in New York State, which Hochul's office hopes will be scrutinized by researchers at the new center. "AI is opening up questions that scientists could not tackle before," said Secunda, who also serves as the board chair of Empire AI, a $500 million public-private partnership. "With Empire AI and researchers across New York, the Center can test systems independently and give public officials evidence they can use." Over 80 leading scientists and researchers on AI systems from across New York state will contribute to the effort, which will be run by the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research at Binghamton University, according to details shared by Hochul's office. The initiative will be led by Jeannette Wing, the executive vice president for research at Columbia University, and Greg Morrisett, the vice provost of Cornell Tech. "We need new techniques that can be applied to this new kind of system with swarms of autonomous agents acting independently and without control. How can you first detect that they're going to do harm, and how can you prevent them from doing harm?" said Wing. "The beauty of what's being proposed is that this state is committing resources to
articles.summary: 纽约州在宾汉姆顿大学设立全美首个州级 AI 安全研究中心，独立测试 AI 系统并培养研究人员。

articles.title: Anthropic Launches New Workplace Features To Take On Microsoft and Google
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from TechCrunch: Anthropic announced new workplace features on Tuesday, including Claude Meetings, which brings Claude into video calls to begin working on tasks while participants are still talking. The company also unveiled Claude Whiteboards and Claude Sheets. The launch of Anthropic's new productivity-focused features comes just a few weeks after OpenAI unveiled a series of workplace tools that allow users to collaborate with ChatGPT to do things like visualize company information and create presentations, as both companies compete to turn their products into office suites of sorts to take on Microsoft and Google. Meta is also joining the competition with its Muse AI agent, which can build mini-apps on the fly to help users complete specific tasks. Here's a summary of each of the offerings Anthropic announced today: Claude Meetings: Allows Claude to join video calls as a visible participant, take notes, answer questions, retrieve information from connected apps, and create plans, timelines, and action items in real time. Available in beta for Team and Enterprise plans, initially supporting Google Meet. Claude Whiteboards: A collaborative visual workspace where teams can brainstorm with Claude, organize ideas into timelines and plans, and turn their work into documents or slide decks. It also integrates with Claude Meetings to build whiteboards during conversations. Claude Sheets: Lets teams create and collaboratively edit spreadsheets with Claude, including budgets and trackers with multiple tabs, formulas, formatting, and dropdown menus. Claude can make changes directly in cells while explaining its edits. Anthropic also announced the general availability of Claude Data (formerly Claude Dashboards) that connects Claude to business systems like CRMs and data warehouses. "Users can ask questions, and Claude responds with dashboards, written data stories, or narrated videos," reports TechCrunch. Additionally, the company announc
articles.summary: Anthropic 推出 Claude Meetings、Whiteboards 和 Sheets 等职场功能，直接挑战微软和谷歌办公套件。

articles.title: Nintendo Is Officially Investing In Game Preservation
articles.content: Nintendo is hiring a digital archivist to help ensure the company's historical records are "preserved for future generations." The 12-month position is tasked with designing and implementing a "structured framework for organizing technical records, engineering documentation, source materials, and institutional knowledge related to legacy systems and platforms." Polygon reports: In the past, Nintendo has drawn criticism from the preservation community. In 2022, the Video Game History Foundation publicly criticized the company for announcing it would be closing the Wii U and 3DS eShops. The foundation released a statement saying that Nintendo's decision was "actively destructive to video game history." The statement also pointed out that Nintendo is part of the Entertainment Software Association, which funds lobbying that prevents a number of preservation efforts. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 任天堂招聘为期 12 个月的数字档案管理员，建立技术记录与源代码等资料的保存框架。

articles.title: Blender 5.3 Released With Nvidia DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction, Vulkan Default
articles.content: Blender 5.3 has been released with support for 3D Gaussian Splats, Nvidia DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction and Vulkan as the default graphics backend on Linux. Phoronix reports: Blender now allows importing Gaussian Splats from PLY, SPZ, and glTF files. Also new to Blender 5.3 is NVIDIA DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction support as a new denoiser. Blender 5.3 also brings support for NVIDIA RTX Spark devices. For the Cycles code in Blender 5.3 the Principled BSDF for shader nodes now supports dispersion. Another notable change with Blender 5.3 is the Vulkan back-end now being the default on Windows (except for Windows on ARM) and Linux systems. Vulkan 1.1 or newer is required and should deliver better performance than OpenGL. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: Blender 5.3 发布，支持 3D Gaussian Splats 导入、Nvidia DLSS 4.5 光线重建，Linux 默认使用 Vulkan 后端。

articles.title: Reddit Is Turning User Conversations Into AI-Powered Product Reviews
articles.content: Reddit is rolling out an AI-powered shopping feature called "Reddit Reviews" that summarizes user conversations about products and turns them into dedicated reviews. TechCrunch reports: Reddit's announcement points to its rules and its latest measures to combat automated abuse and spam, as well as its practice involving community moderators, as tools it will use to keep the reviews on the site legit. The Reddit Reviews feature itself taps into AI to organize the conversations people are having where they describe their product experiences. These posts will often see users discussing how a product works for them, or why it fails, or what the trade-offs are that someone should consider before buying. The company has been testing the product reviews feature since February, initially with U.S. users in areas like Electronics, Video Games, and Health & Beauty products. In September, Reddit expanded the test to include the Home & Garden and Fashion & Apparel categories as well. Now, the company says Reddit Reviews is rolling out to all U.S. users on iOS, Android, and web, with an initial selection focused on around 10,000 products. Over time, it will roll out to more categories and expand beyond the U.S. To use the feature, Reddit users can search for a product or category in the app's search bar or click on a highlighted product name they see in someone's comment. From there, the user is taken to a screen where important conversations are summarized under a "what people are saying" heading. This will also include a visual breakdown that shows how many of those comments are positive, negative, or mixed, and what sort of things people said they liked or disliked about the item. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

When it announced its acquisition, Uber said SpotHero offered garages and lots across more than 400 cities in the US and Canada, but the company isn't offering all of them at launch. For now, Uber says Uber Parking will be available in Chicago, Nashville, San Francisco, Atlanta, Austin, Boston, Dallas, Denver, Los Angeles, Miami, New York City, Philadelphia, San Diego, Seattle and Washington DC. articles.title: We Migrated 10,144 Tests from Jest to Vitest in 3 Weeks: The Honest, AI-Assisted Truth
articles.content: A note on the Vitest version: This migration was carried out in August 2026, using Vitest 4 . All the figures, benchmarks, configuration details, and lessons described in this article refer to Vitest 4, not Vitest 5. Migrating a test runner is rarely a magic "swap and go" operation. Our experience moving our entire frontend test suite from Jest to Vitest was a real engineering undertaking, filled with bottlenecks, meticulous pool tuning, unmasked bugs, one rollback, and one optimization we shipped and then had to take back. Over the course of about three weeks, our frontend team migrated eight repositories. We didn't settle for file counts; we ran every suite end-to-end to get the real numbers. Here is the exact scale of what we achieved: 10,144 executed unit tests, real numbers from actually running the suites, not file counts. 1,799 test files across 8 repositories. 0 repos left in a half-migrated state. ~3 weeks to complete the entire effort, migrations plus the tuning that followed. ~$751 estimated AI token cost for the Claude Code sessions we could trace to this work. See the caveats on that number below: it's a rough upper bound, not a bill. This is the story of what actually happened, drawn directly from our git history, PR bodies, and session logs, to help you navigate your own migration. To save you some of the pain we went through, we also published a generalized version of the AI automation skill we ended up wishing we'd had from day one: github.com/Subito-it/articles-code/tree/main/jest-to-vitest-migration . Why Jest started hurting We didn't decide to migrate just because "Jest is slow" in the abstract. We migrated because maintaining it had become an active, recurring tax on our engineering time. We also wanted to be on the side of where the ecosystem was heading, since Vitest was fast becoming the default choice for new Vite/Next.js projects. 1. The CommonJS vs. ESM nightmare By default, next/jest skips transforming anything inside node_modules , so when a dependency ships an ESM-only update, Jest's CommonJS require() fails. We found ourselves hand-patching transformIgnorePatterns regexes to allow-list specific packages. Here's the exact code comment from our config, verbatim: // ESM-only node_modules that Jest must transform. next/jest overwrites any // user-supplied transformIgnorePatterns to skip all of node_modules, so we // allow-list these on the resolved config instead. const esmPackagesToTransform = [ ' cookie ' ]; Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Separately, and about six weeks before we'd even decided to migrate: a major version bump of uuid shipped as pure ESM and broke Jest outright. The real commit message: "uuid v14 ships as pure ESM which breaks Jest (CommonJS). Replace the single usage of uuid() ... with the native crypto.randomUUID() ... removing the dependency entirely." Rather than fight the transform config again, the team just deleted the dependency. When your test runner is dictating your dependency

articles.title: Repo-Atlas - Any GitHub user’s work, mapped and clustered, with stale favorites flagged.
articles.content: Type a GitHub username, get the map of what they've actually built: repos clustered by topic, the highlight of each group, and stars over time. Live: https://evoluteur.github.io/repo-atlas/ · permalink per user: ?u=<username> The map. Every public repo as a disc (area ∝ stars), grouped into regions of repos that share topics. Hover for details, click to open the repo. Groups by stars. The legend ranks the regions by the stars they hold, so you see where the attention actually sits. Highlights. The most-starred repo in each group as a card, with its description, language and live-demo link. Hover a card to find its group on the map; the share card lists the top three. Stars over time. Without a token: stars held today, stacked by the year each repo was born. With a token: real cumulative star history per group, from stargazer dates. Share. A 1200×630 card for social posts and a permalink. Each repo's topics are normalised (plurals folded, generic tags like javascript , svg , ui dropped) and hyphenated topics also contribute their parts ( sacred-geometry → sacred , geometry ). Tokens are weighted by inverse document frequency across the account. Tokens used once, or by more than 45% of repos, carry no signal and are dropped. Repos with almost no topics fall back to description words. Repos are compared by cosine similarity and merged bottom-up (average linkage) until no two groups are more than 0.16 alike. The eight groups holding the most stars get a color and a two-word name (the tokens most frequent inside the group and rarest outside it). Everything else folds into loners . All of this is in src/atlas.js : pure functions, no DOM, tested with node --test . Everything runs in the browser against the public GitHub REST API. The map and the highlights work anonymously (60 requests/hour per IP; a typical account takes 2). GitHub only lists when each star was given to authenticated callers, so the star-history chart needs a token. A fine-grained token with no extra permissions is enough. It is kept in sessionStorage for the tab and only sent to api.github.com . Big repos are sampled: every stargazer page for repos under 500 stars, otherwise the first, last and three evenly spaced pages. Each fetched star is an exact (count, date) point; months in between are interpolated. Results are cached in localStorage (repos 1 hour, star history 24 hours). If the API can't be reached (rate limit, offline), the page lets you paste the JSON from api.github.com/users/<login>/repos?per_page=100 and maps that instead. No build step. Serve the folder and open it: npx serve . # or: python3 -m http.server open http://localhost:3000/?u=evoluteur npm test # clustering, highlights and timeline math npm run build # dist/repo-atlas.html: one self-contained file index.html page shell src/atlas.js clustering, highlights, timelines (pure, Node-testable) src/github.js REST client: repos, sampled stargazer pages src/charts.js D3: circle-pack map, birth-year columns, stacked star

articles.title: SVAR Gantt v2.8 for React, Svelte, Vue: upgraded scheduling engine & live updates
articles.content: We’re excited to announce version 2.8 of the SVAR Gantt chart components for React , Vue , and Svelte . This release makes the scheduling engine more than a display layer: it now handles many of the scheduling scenarios project managers deal with in real projects. With this update, SVAR Gantt PRO becomes a stronger tool for project planning and resource allocation. In version 2.8, we introduce an upgraded scheduling engine that takes auto-scheduling in SVAR Gantt PRO to the next level: Auto-scheduling across all four dependency types: FS, SS, FF, and SF. Critical path and slack now calculated based on all dependency types. Six scheduling constraints set the boundaries a plan must respect. Resource-driven scheduling calculates task dates from the working calendars of assigned people. Faster scheduling for auto-scheduling and critical path, which now run much faster with thousands of tasks. To make SVAR Gantt a more complete tool for project management and resource planning, we also added: Extended resource planning with a resource histogram and drag-and-drop resource assignment. New project tracking features , such as the progress line and S-curve. Sub-grid panel for task details shown to the right of the Gantt chart. Real-time server updates that support multi-user editing and collaboration. 🔹 See full changelog : React Gantt • Vue Gantt • Svelte Gantt 🔹 View demos for v2.8 : React Gantt • Vue Gantt • Svelte Gantt The following sections cover what ships in SVAR Gantt PRO . The MIT edition also gains three features of its own, listed at the end. Upgraded Scheduling Engine We’ve upgraded the scheduling engine of SVAR Gantt PRO to provide automatic scheduling logic for project planning: All four link types in auto-scheduling and the critical path Auto-scheduling previously supported only Finish-to-Start links, but in 2.8 we added support for Start-to-Start, Finish-to-Finish, and Start-to-Finish links, with lag applied to every link type. All four link types now affect dates, slack, and the critical path , which means overlapping work can be planned as it happens in real projects. When a linked task changes, the engine always recalculates the dates of its dependent tasks. 👉 Auto-scheduling demo: React • Svelte • Vue Manual and inactive tasks For more flexibility, we also added two task modes that take tasks out of auto-scheduling: manual and inactive tasks. The inactiveTasks feature enables support for inactive tasks in the grid and editor; to make a specific task inactive, set its inactive field to true . 我是一个喜欢记录各种事情的人，但是现有的记录软件不能满足我记录电脑活动的需求（ActivityWatch、Qbserve 不好看，Timing 太贵而且复杂。还有很多软件在我看来是过度记录，既占储存又费电……）。所以出于自己的记录需求，我制作了 Mac 上的原生活动记录 app「日影」。

我把易用和美观排在首位，「日影」会自动记录用户的活动，所以不需要占用精力，容易持续下来。并且通过键鼠活动和前台播放来推断用户是否在真的使用 Mac，以提高记录的精确性，同时不需要请求额外的系统权限。

在统计页面里，可以看到自己某天某月在做什么，看到自己的使用趋势等等。我花了不少精力来把页面做好看。

![]( https://i.imgur.com/8eJM5eY.png) 
![]( https://i.imgur.com/odR2phi.png) 
![]( https://i.imgur.com/1A0eVt2.png) 
![]( https://i.imgur.com/cnQEw5Z.png) 
![]( https://i.imgur.com/JjtVXSp.png) 
![]( https://i.imgur.com/5aFCrRG.png) 

除了基础的记录功能，我还思考怎么发挥 Mac 的特色。日影具有和系统日历的集成——自动把项目活动写入系统日历，这样的话就可以在日历里回顾自己的一天了。

![]( https://i.imgur.com/MwbAN8D.png) 

日影还有提醒功能，比如站立提醒（持续使用电脑后提醒站立）、专注提醒（基于用户活动自动开始番茄钟提醒）、限额提醒、目标提醒、时间感知提醒（女友有 ADHD，这个功能帮她感知时间）等等。相比其他的手动计时器，由于知道用户在用什么 App，所以日影会根据规则自动开启计时器，要方便一点。

![]( https://i.imgur.com/TzZVbbx.png) 

## 隐私

记录是在本地进行的，默认不会上传任何记录数据。主动开启备份后，可以将数据安全备份到 iCloud。备份多台 Mac 到同一目录后，支持在本机同时查看其他 Mac 的数据。

更详细的隐私说明见看官网的[隐私政策]( https://hikage.app/zh-CN/privacy/) 。

## 官网和软件下载

https://hikage.app/zh-CN/

articles.title: 外企外包也许是大龄失业人员的最好归宿
articles.content:
入职一家外企外包几个月，谈谈感受。

我们组一共 12 人，全部 95 前，还有几个 80 后，只有 3 个是正式的，其余全是外包。时间最长的在这边干了有 6 年多，稳定性不错

工作极度轻松，是我工作以来最轻松的，之前在互联网公司上班的肯定不太适应这个节奏。以前公司排期一周的任务这边至少排一个月，做不完继续延期。有几位负责做重构的同事，他们的任务已经排到 2028 年了

不打卡不管考勤，基本就是想来就来想走就走，我们一般 10 点到 6 点，午休两小时。不想来的随时可以居家办公，没人管。我们组有不少家在外地的，长期居家办公，我到现在还没见过真人。非常适合大龄有家庭有孩子的

收入肯定比不了大厂，和一般民企差不多，10 年经验年收入税前 40-50w 左右，到手也就 30 多，但是胜在轻松，这个性价比还是可以的

福利待遇不如正式员工，没有那么多的年假，但是随时请假，随时申请 wfh ，看起来差别不大。

外企/外企外包不卡学历不卡年龄，只要懂一点点英语就行，真的对大龄非常友好了，强烈推荐失业的 v 友冲
articles.summary: 作者分享入职外企外包数月感受：工作轻松、不打卡、可长期居家，认为这可能是大龄失业人员的好归宿。

articles.title: 马上结婚了，但是吵架了！
articles.content:
## 背景：

女朋友对我很好，人也很好，经常给我买东西，我给她买的东西有，但没有她给我买的多
平时住在一起，大的花销一般是我出，但是最后出的应该也差不多，没太计较这个

彩礼、三金：说的是 18.8w ，反正多少来着，没记清，我转给女朋友 20 万。

马上结婚了，因为时间比较急，还没有买三金，婚礼也是在村里办的，也能省一些钱

订婚，彩礼的主要花费都是我出，我父母没出，他们没啥钱，但是也不想着多赚些钱，他们出了家里的酒席钱，车队、旅馆。

我父母没出钱，一方面是因为他们没啥钱，另一方面也是我觉着他们没啥钱，留点钱有安全感，不太想让他们出。

我女朋友现在工资比我高一些。

女朋友对我父母不出钱很有意见。

## 矛盾点：

1.父母改口费，女朋友说，他们父母 1 人准备要给 1 万 1 ，我问了我妈，说家里一般都是 1 人给 1 千 1 ，我想着 1 万 1 太多，给父母的压力也比较大，还想着和女朋友再沟通下，结果下班时，说到买房，我说我不想背房贷，北京的房子也太贵了，这点她不开心，后来就不太愉快，后来她又问我改口费这个，她问了我好多次了，我因为犯懒或则不知道咋说也好，就说不知道，这次她问时，我赌气说 1 千 1 ，然后她就和她妈那边说都给 1 千 1 。然后情绪就更不好了。

我之所以说 1 千 1 ，主要是对我父母不努力的责怪也好，还是怎样，类似于那种你们不努力，到儿子结婚一分钱也没有，还想要体面，体面没了。

但是其实我父母也不是说不努力，他们挺节省的，但是经常吵架，核心不是想着怎么赚钱，我也想改变他们，但是我无能为力，我妈他们虽然钱不多，但是也可以 1 人给 1 万 1 ，只是因为钱不多，有些压力。他们还要养着我爷爷。

2.亲戚改口费，婚礼典礼拜谁，女朋友比较社恐，本来说不拜我的那些亲戚了，就拜我爸妈就行了，结果我爸妈又说我的那些亲戚想上典礼给改口费，我女朋友说改口费多少钱呢，我说 1 人给 1 百，她说他们那边亲戚都是给 600 多的。这也导火索

## 直接导火索：

我直接给我妈打电话，说不拜那些亲戚了，我妈问了几遍，我都说不拜了，这也是之前答应我女朋友的，我妈说也耽误不了多长时间，我说不拜了，真不拜了。我女朋友就在旁边。


1. 我父母的人生我管不了，他们努力赚钱与否，有多少钱我也控制不了。
2. 儿子结婚父母就一定要出钱吗？我以前一直认为出不出都行，但是彩礼默认是父母出的呢？有次去买烟，老板问彩礼多少钱，我说 18 万多，老板说，不少啊，反正都是给了小两口，也没给别人，其实这钱都是我出的。
3. 我确实对女朋友关心不如她关系我多，但是我也没想着白嫖什么的，或则坑她什么的。她觉得我们全家都在坑她。



我要给女朋友写小作文哄哄了。

大伙分析下，都有啥问题呢？
articles.summary: 用户发帖讲述婚前因彩礼、三金和父母出资问题与女友吵架，寻求网友对双方经济分担与家庭责任的建议。

# 大纲

到了外面女的见我还是不给于是打算不演了，又是出示微信余额(没看清实际余额)又说什么没人看得上你之类的话。

今天早上摸鱼摸着摸着就看到邮箱来了新邮件 打开一看是律师函？？？一脸懵

UDRP 域名争议，案号 HK‑2602201 ，域名 `aiping.icu`

我是该域名原始注册人，在 Cloudflare 注册。收到 ADNDRC 香港办事处发来的 UDRP 投诉通知。

现状：我搭建的是**大模型 API 公开测评榜单网站**，和投诉方 [aiping.cn]( https://aiping.cn) 都不是同一个东西，对方是售卖 token 的。

投诉方主张自己拥有 “AIPING” 未注册商标，要求把域名转移过去，说我不是第一时间注册人，我看了 WHOIS 第一注册人就是我在 cf 上购买的时间。

答辩截止时间 **2026‑11‑30**，程序要求提交英文 Form‑R 答辩书。

有点懵，想请教大佬们 帮忙支招= =
